questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the actual skill being tested by an architect-style scenario question?
options: Recalling the single correct factual definition of a term
Noticing which constraint in the scenario's wording rules out an otherwise-obvious answer, and justifying the recommendation against those constraints
Typing the fastest among several candidates
Memorizing every Salesforce governor limit by edition
questions.explain: These questions are built from a scenario with embedded constraints -- the skill is naming which constraint eliminates each plausible-but-wrong alternative, not just reciting a fact.

questions.q: In Scenario 1 (the unattended nightly ERP sync with no human present and a desire to avoid certificate management), why does this lesson rule out both Authorization Code and JWT Bearer flow?
options: Authorization Code assumes a browser consent step (no human is present); JWT Bearer depends on certificate management (which the team wants to avoid) -- leaving Client Credentials flow
Both flows are deprecated and cannot be used in any Salesforce org
Neither flow supports ERP integrations under any circumstances
Authorization Code and JWT Bearer are actually the same flow under different names
questions.explain: Each ruled-out flow is eliminated by a specific stated constraint: no human present rules out Authorization Code's consent step, and avoiding certificates rules out JWT Bearer -- Client Credentials fits what's left.

questions.q: In Scenario 3, what two separate claims does this lesson say need to be challenged when a partner argues their webhook doesn't need signature verification?
options: That the data isn't sensitive (confuses confidentiality with integrity/availability) and that the URL is private (security through obscurity -- Site URLs are discoverable)
That the webhook is slow and that it costs too much to implement
That Salesforce technically prohibits webhook signature verification
That only JWT Bearer flow requires signature verification
questions.explain: The 'URL is private' claim is security through obscurity (URLs are discoverable, not secret), and the 'data isn't sensitive' claim addresses confidentiality only -- it ignores that unsigned data can still be forged or flooded, which is an integrity/availability risk independent of secrecy.

questions.q: In Scenario 4 (the four-year-old System Administrator integration user), what does this lesson say 'it's never caused a problem' actually describes?
options: Proof that the integration user has no meaningful risk at all
Absence of detected misuse, not absence of risk -- the blast radius if that credential is ever compromised is still the entire org, regardless of past history
Confirmation that least privilege doesn't apply to integration users that have run successfully for years
Evidence that the integration's access should be expanded further
questions.explain: The scenario tests whether least privilege is understood as a standing risk independent of observed history -- no detected problem yet doesn't shrink the blast radius a compromised System Administrator-level credential would have.

questions.q: What is the four-step reusable structure this lesson gives for answering any scenario question?
options: Guess the answer, defend it at all costs, ignore counterarguments, move on

Identify every stated constraint, name the specific constraint that rules out each plausible alternative, state the recommendation tied to the surviving constraints, and note any remaining risk the recommendation doesn't fully resolve
Only name the final recommendation, with no justification required
List every Salesforce feature that could conceivably apply, without narrowing
questions.explain: The reusable structure is explicitly: identify constraints, rule out alternatives by name, justify the recommendation against what survived, and flag any remaining open risk -- this is what separates a defensible answer from a confident guess.
